seo_title: Fire Damage 101: Protect Your Home and Your Insurance Claim
meta_description: Fire damage 101 for Texas homeowners: what fire insurance covers, how to protect your home, what to do after a fire, and how fire damage estimates work.
h1: Fire Damage 101: Protect Your Home and Recover After a Fire Loss
excerpt: Fire damage goes beyond what burned: smoke, heat and water damage matter too. Learn how to protect your home, what insurance covers and how fire damage estimates work.
key_takeaways: Fire damage includes flame, smoke, heat and firefighting water damage.
Document every room before cleanup and keep damaged items until inspected.
Carrier estimates often miss smoke migration, HVAC and code-required work.
If coverage is accepted but the amount is disputed, appraisal may resolve it.
body_html:
Fire damage includes everything a fire leaves behind: burned materials, smoke and soot residue, heat damage, and water damage from firefighting. Most Texas homeowners policies cover sudden, accidental fire loss to the home, contents and additional living expenses. Protecting your home, documenting the loss and getting an accurate fire damage estimate are the keys to a full recovery.

A house fire changes everything in minutes. Beyond the emotional toll, it leaves a complicated insurance claim that involves the structure, your belongings, temporary housing and often months of repairs. This guide covers what fire damage really includes, how to protect your home, what to do in the first days after a fire, how fire damage estimates work, and what to do if the carrier's number falls short.

What is fire damage?

Fire damage is broader than the area that burned. Insurers and estimators generally look at four categories:

TypeWhat it looks likeWhy it matters
Direct flame damageCharred framing, drywall, roofing, contentsUsually requires removal and replacement
Smoke and soot damageResidue on walls, ceilings, HVAC, contentsCan spread throughout the house, far from the fire
Heat damageWarped windows, melted fixtures, damaged wiringOften missed because it is less visible
Water and chemical damageSoaked drywall, flooring, insulation; extinguisher residueFirefighting can damage rooms the fire never reached

Smoke and odor are where many fire claims become disputed. Soot can travel through HVAC ducts, wall cavities and attics, contaminating rooms on the other side of the house. Cleaning may work in some areas; in others, replacement is the only way to eliminate odor.

How to protect your home from fire

Prevention reduces both risk and claim complexity. Practical steps include:

  • Install smoke alarms on every level and in sleeping areas, and test them monthly.
  • Keep fire extinguishers in the kitchen, garage and near fireplaces.
  • Have heating systems, chimneys and dryer vents inspected and cleaned regularly.
  • Have older electrical panels and wiring evaluated by a licensed electrician.
  • Never leave cooking or candles unattended.
  • Clear dry brush and debris around the house, especially in rural and wildfire-prone areas.
  • Store important documents and a home inventory outside the house or in the cloud.
Tip: Walk through your home once a year and record a video of every room, closet and the exterior. That one file makes a fire contents claim dramatically easier.

Fire risks for Texas homeowners

Texas faces fire threats beyond the typical kitchen or electrical fire. Drought and high winds make wildfire a real risk in the Panhandle, West Texas and parts of Central Texas. The 2024 Panhandle wildfires were a reminder of how quickly grass fires can reach homes and ranch properties near Amarillo and surrounding communities. Homeowners in those areas can find local claim help through our Amarillo insurance appraiser page.

Winter cold snaps also increase fire risk as space heaters, fireplaces and generators run hard. Summer heat strains electrical systems and air conditioning units. Wherever you live in Texas, check your local burn bans and county fire guidance during dry periods. The Texas Department of Insurance also publishes consumer information on homeowners coverage and claims.

What should you do after a house fire?

  1. Stay safe. Do not re-enter until the fire department says it is safe.
  2. Notify your insurer promptly. Report the loss and get a claim number.
  3. Get the fire report. Request a copy from the fire department.
  4. Secure the property. Board up openings and tarp the roof to prevent further damage, as most policies require. Keep receipts.
  5. Document everything. Photograph and video every room before cleanup. A Matterport 3D scan preserves the entire house before debris removal.
  6. Track living expenses. Keep receipts for hotels, meals and other added costs.
  7. Do not throw things away until the adjuster has seen them or you have documented them thoroughly.
  8. Start a contents inventory listing items, approximate age and replacement cost.

Our claim documentation checklist lists everything worth collecting.

Be cautious with anyone who shows up uninvited right after a fire offering to handle everything. Take time to check licenses, reviews and contracts before signing with a restoration company or contractor. Read any assignment or authorization carefully, and keep copies of everything you sign. You can make emergency decisions to protect the property without committing to a full rebuild contract on the first day.

What does homeowners insurance cover for fire loss?

Most Texas homeowners policies cover fire as a named or open peril. Typical coverage parts include:

  • Dwelling (Coverage A): the structure and attached features.
  • Other structures (Coverage B): detached garages, fences and sheds.
  • Personal property (Coverage C): furniture, clothing, electronics and other contents.
  • Loss of use (Coverage D): additional living expenses while the home is uninhabitable.

Replacement cost policies usually pay actual cash value first and release recoverable depreciation after repairs or replacement. See recoverable depreciation explained to understand how much may be held back and how to recover it.

Common exclusions and limits

  • Intentional fires set by an insured.
  • Vacancy limitations if the home was unoccupied for an extended period.
  • Sub-limits on jewelry, cash, collectibles and other special items.
  • Code upgrade costs beyond any ordinance and law limit.
  • Damage from wear, neglect or gradual issues unrelated to the fire.

Read your declarations page and endorsements to confirm your limits and deductibles.

How a fire damage estimate works

A fire damage estimate is a line-item breakdown of every task needed to restore the home, usually written in Xactimate or Symbility. A thorough estimate covers:

  • Board-up, tarping and emergency services.
  • Demolition and debris removal.
  • Structural repairs to framing, roofing and sheathing.
  • Smoke and soot cleaning, sealing and deodorization throughout the house.
  • HVAC and duct cleaning or replacement.
  • Electrical and plumbing repairs, often with code upgrades.
  • Drywall, insulation, paint, flooring, cabinets and trim.
  • Contents cleaning, pack-out, storage and replacement.
  • Overhead and profit for a general contractor coordinating multiple trades.

Carrier estimates often fall short on smoke migration, cleaning versus replacement decisions, HVAC contamination and code-required electrical work. An independent Xactimate estimate lets you compare scope line by line.

An illustrative example

Suppose a kitchen fire burns cabinets and part of the ceiling. The carrier's estimate replaces the kitchen and cleans the adjoining living room. Your contractor finds soot in the HVAC system, smoke odor in upstairs bedrooms and heat-damaged wiring in the wall behind the stove. Those items can easily add up to more than the original kitchen scope, and each needs photos, test results or a contractor's written findings to support it.

Clean or replace? The biggest fire damage dispute

On many fire claims, the largest disagreement is not about what burned, but about what can be cleaned. Carriers often price cleaning and sealing for smoke-affected walls, ceilings, cabinets and contents. Owners and contractors may find that odor returns, residue keeps bleeding through paint, or materials are too damaged to restore.

Factors that usually decide the question include:

  • Material type: porous materials such as insulation, carpet pad, upholstery and unsealed wood absorb smoke more readily than hard surfaces.
  • Residue type: some fires leave dry soot that cleans relatively easily, while others leave oily or protein residue that is much harder to remove.
  • Heat exposure: heat can warp, discolor or weaken materials even where there is no visible char.
  • Testing results: cleaning tests or post-cleaning inspections show whether restoration actually worked.

Document cleaning attempts, keep notes on lingering odor, and ask your restoration contractor for written findings when cleaning fails. That evidence turns a vague complaint into a specific, supportable line item.

Special considerations for fire damage claims

Fire claims bring a few issues that storm claims rarely do. Contents claims can involve hundreds or thousands of items, so a room-by-room approach and help from family members can make the inventory manageable. Pack-out companies may move salvageable items to storage for cleaning; ask for their inventory list and photos. Code upgrades are common because damaged electrical and plumbing systems often must meet current code when repaired, which is where ordinance and law coverage matters. Finally, mortgage companies are usually listed on claim checks for structural repairs, so contact your lender early to understand how funds will be released during reconstruction.

What if your fire claim is underpaid?

Start by requesting the carrier's full estimate and comparing it with your contractor's. Submit a written rebuttal with photos and documentation for each missing item, and ask for a reinspection. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542 generally requires carriers to acknowledge claims within 15 days and to decide within 15 business days after receiving requested information, with extensions possible.

If the carrier agrees the fire is covered but still disputes the amount, most Texas policies include an appraisal clause. Each side names an appraiser, an umpire resolves disagreements, and the award sets the amount of loss. Appraisers do not decide coverage questions. This is general information, not legal advice. For commercial buildings, see fire damage commercial insurance claims.

Next steps after fire damage

Recovering from a fire takes time, but a methodical approach protects the value of your claim: stay safe, secure the property, document everything, track expenses, and review every estimate carefully before accepting it. Ask questions in writing whenever something in the estimate is unclear, and do not assume the first number is final. Fire claims are often revised several times as hidden damage is uncovered during demolition.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover smoke damage without a fire in my home?
faqs.a: Many policies cover smoke damage from a sudden fire nearby, such as a neighbor's house fire or a wildfire, because smoke is commonly a covered peril. Coverage depends on your policy wording and the source of the smoke. Document residue, odor and affected items, and report the loss promptly so the carrier can inspect.

faqs.q: How long does a fire insurance claim take in Texas?
faqs.a: Simple fire claims may settle in a few weeks, while major losses involving reconstruction, contents and living expenses often take months. Texas Chapter 542 sets deadlines for carriers to acknowledge, decide and pay claims once they receive requested information. Organized documentation and prompt responses on your side help keep the claim moving.

faqs.q: Who prepares the fire damage estimate for an insurance claim?
faqs.a: The carrier's adjuster usually writes the initial estimate, often in Xactimate. Your contractor, a restoration company or an independent estimator can prepare a competing line-item estimate. Comparing both side by side shows where scope, quantities or pricing differ and is the starting point for negotiating or, if needed, appraisal.

faqs.q: Should I throw away fire-damaged belongings right away?
faqs.a: Not until they are documented. Photograph each item, record brand, age and approximate value, and keep damaged items until the adjuster has seen them or confirmed in writing that they can be discarded. Throwing items away too early can make it harder to prove the contents portion of your claim.

faqs.q: Can I stay in a hotel after a fire, and will insurance pay?
faqs.a: If your home is uninhabitable because of a covered fire, loss of use or additional living expense coverage generally pays reasonable increased costs, such as a hotel or rental and extra meal expenses, up to your policy limits. Keep every receipt and confirm with your adjuster what types of expenses are covered.
